text: Castellan Retail's SOC wants two new detection rules live before the next pen test: one for a well-known SQL injection scanning tool, and one for the kind of beaconing behavior a real command-and-control implant produces. Both build directly on Lesson 7's Suricata syntax, applied to attack patterns that actually show up in SOC alert queues.

Every Suricata rule has the same three parts: an action like alert or drop, a header specifying protocol, source, direction, and destination, and a set of options in parentheses carrying the message, the match conditions, and a unique sid. Both of this lab's rules get built against that exact structure, piece by piece.

Sqlmap is a widely used SQL injection tool that identifies itself in the HTTP User-Agent header by default. The rule uses http.user_agent as a sticky buffer so the content match only scans that one header, with nocase added so an attacker capitalizing it differently can't slip past a case-sensitive match.

A real implant rarely announces itself in a header — it beacons, checking in on a regular interval with a small, consistently sized request. Dsize flags requests smaller than legitimate traffic to that path would ever be, and threshold waits until the same source repeats the pattern twenty times in five minutes before it alerts.

A rule that's too broad causes alert fatigue, so before either rule ships, the SOC checks it against reality: no legitimate internal tool sends sqlmap in its User-Agent, so Rule 1 ships as-is, but Chapter 6's authorized vulnerability scanner does hit the beacon pattern's URI during its own scheduled scans, so Rule 2 gets an exception for that scanner's source IP first.

Rule 2's size-and-frequency match is more durable than Rule 1's exact string match, because it survives an attacker switching to a different C2 tool next month. Next up, a full case study showing where a rule exactly like Rule 2 fits inside a real, slow data-exfiltration detection chain.
